The canvas was rolled up twice in its first hundred years and has needed repeated treatment for flaking paint since. It came to England in 1806.

VAULT-878.note: The panel is a single piece of walnut four to five millimetres thick, most likely cut from the same tree as the one Leonardo used for La Belle Ferronnière. His fingerprints are in the paint of the face and the animal's head. The sitter, Cecilia Gallerani, was about sixteen and the mistress of his employer, the Duke of Milan. The background was probably bluish-grey before it was painted over in black. The Nazis seized the picture in 1939 and Hans Frank hung it in his offices; Allied troops found it at his country home in Bavaria.

VAULT-892.note: An inventory of 1499 records this panel in the Florence palace of Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, hanging above a large piece of furniture with its bottom edge at about eye level. Most scholars now connect it to his marriage on 19 July 1482. Botticelli painted some 500 identified species of plant into it, including about 190 different flowers. A second inventory in 1503 notes a large white frame. The name Primavera comes from Giorgio Vasari, who saw the painting at the Medici villa at Castello by 1550.

VAULT-907.note: Delacroix took the subject from Lord Byron's play Sardanapalus, published six years before he showed the painting at the Paris Salon of 1827, where it divided opinion. In 1844 he made a smaller replica, now in Philadelphia. Hector Berlioz wrote a cantata on the subject in 1830, and Franz Liszt began an opera after seeing the painting and abandoned it with one act complete.

VAULT-923.note: The room is the studio Matisse had built for himself in 1909. He first painted the canvas a pale yellow, then went over it with a thin coat of red. The pale outlines of the furniture are not drawn lines at all: they are narrow bands of the yellow underneath that he left uncovered. Shortly before he painted it he had seen an exhibition of Islamic art in Munich and travelled to Seville, Córdoba, Granada, St. Petersburg and Moscow.

VAULT-937.note: The three Limbourg brothers and the duke who employed them all died in 1416, and the book was left unfinished and unbound. Another painter added to it in the 1440s, and Jean Colombe completed it between 1485 and 1489 for the Duke of Savoy, who paid him 25 gold pieces. It has 206 leaves of calfskin, 30 centimetres by 21.5, with 66 large miniatures and 65 small ones. The painters used about ten colours besides black and white, with extremely small brushes and probably a lens. The Musée Condé withdrew the book from display in the 1980s.
